bib.title: Efficient and robust approximate nearest neighbor search using Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs
bib.venue: preprint (arXiv manuscript headed 'submitted to the IEEE'; published IEEE TPAMI 2020)

question: Can a fully graph-based multilayer proximity-graph index give logarithmic-complexity approximate K-nearest-neighbour search that is robust on low-dimensional and clustered data, where NSW degrades?
hypothesis: Separating links by length scale into layers (random exponentially decaying level per element) plus a diversity heuristic for neighbour selection removes NSW's polylogarithmic scaling and its failures on low-dimensional or clustered data.
contributions: explicit selection of the graph's enter-point node
separation of links by different scales
use of an advanced heuristic to select the neighbors

method.summary: HNSW builds a multilayer proximity graph by incremental insertion; each element gets a random max layer l = floor(-ln(unif(0,1))*mL), is linked to M neighbours per layer chosen by a diversity heuristic, and search descends greedily from the top layer with ef=1 then does beam search with ef at layer 0. Implemented in C++ in nmslib and compared on ann-benchmarks vector sets, nmslib general-space sets, and 200M SIFT against Faiss PQ.

eval.protocol: Best result chosen per recall range for each algorithm, starting from testbed defaults; ann-benchmark testbed for vector data, nmslib scripts for general spaces, Faiss built-in scripts for 200M SIFT. No seeds, repeats or significance tests stated.

results.claim: HNSW search complexity is O(log N) under an exact Delaunay graph with degree capped by a constant.
results.setup: Theory assuming exact Delaunay graphs; simulations on low-dimensional (d=4) data only
results.quote: And since the expectation of the maximum layer index by the construction scales as O(log(N)), the overall complexity scaling is O(log(N)), in agreement with the simulations on low dimensional datasets.

results.claim: Expected steps per layer are bounded independent of dataset size.
results.quote: the expected number of steps in a layer is bounded by a sum of geometric progression S =1/(1-exp(-mL)), which is independent of the dataset size.

results.claim: The authors concede the approximate-graph resilience is unproven for high dimensions.
results.setup: d=128 empirical check infeasible since Delaunay degree grows exponentially with dimension
results.quote: Further analitical evidence is required to confirm whether the resilience of Delaunay graph aproximations generalizes to higher dimensional spaces.

results.claim: Construction time scales as N log N for low-dimensional data.
results.quote: at least for relatively low dimensional datasets the construction time scales as O(N∙log(N)).

results.claim: On 200M SIFT query time deviates from pure logarithmic scaling.
results.quote: Note that the scaling deviates from the pure logarithm, possibly due to relatively high dimensionality of the dataset.

results.claim: Suggested mL is 1/ln(M), matching skip list p=1/M.
results.setup: simulations on 10M random d=4, 100k random d=1024, 5M SIFT (Figs 3-5)
results.quote: A simple choice for the optimal mL is 1/ln(M), this corresponds to the skip list parameter p=1/M with an average single element overlap between the layers.

results.claim: Mmax0 = 2*M is a good choice; Mmax0 = M gives a very strong penalty at high recall.
results.quote: Simulations also suggest that 2∙M is a good choice for Mmax0: setting the parameter higher leads to performance degradation and excessive memory usage.

results.claim: M is the only meaningful construction parameter; reasonable range 5 to 48.
results.quote: The only meaningful construction parameter left for the user is M. A reasonable range of M is from 5 to 48.

results.claim: efConstruction should give construction-time recall near unity; 0.95 enough for most use cases.
results.quote: (0.95 is enough for the most use-cases)

results.claim: 10M SIFT index builds in 3 minutes at efConstruction=100.
results.quote: a reasonable quality index can be constructed for efConstruction=100 on a 4X 2.4 GHz 10-core Xeon E5-4650 v2 CPU server in just 3 minutes.

results.claim: Index memory is about 60-450 bytes per object excluding data.
results.setup: M between 6 and 48, 4-byte link ids, up to ~4 billion elements
results.quote: This means that the typical memory requirements for the index (excluding the size of the data) are about 60-450 bytes per object, which is in a good agreement with the simulations.

results.claim: Per-element memory formula.
HNSW outperforms rivals by a large margin on SIFT, GloVe, DEEP and CoPhIR; only slightly faster than Annoy at high recall on d=4.
results.setup: ann-benchmarks, 10-NN, 1000 queries, single thread, curves in Fig 13
results.quote: For SIFT, GloVE, DEEP and CoPhIR datasets Hierarchical NSW clearly outperforms the rivals by a large margin.

results.claim: Improvement over NSW is almost 3 orders of magnitude on Wiki-8 (JS divergence).
results.quote: The strongest enhancement over NSW, almost by 3 orders of magnitude is observed for the dataset with the lowest dimensionality, the wiki-8 with JS-divergence.

results.claim: HNSW needs significantly more RAM than Faiss PQ but gets higher accuracy, much faster search and construction.
results.quote: Even though Hierarchical NSW requires significantly more RAM, it can achieve much higher accuracy, while offering a massive advance in search speed and much faster index construction.

results.claim: Heuristic neighbour selection fixes failure on clustered data; closest-neighbour linking sticks at cluster boundaries.
results.quote: the Hierarchical NSW algorithm fails to achieve a high recall for clustered data because the search stucks at the clusters boundaries.

limits: Complexity proof assumes exact Delaunay graphs and bounded degree; approximate graph supported only by low-dimensional simulations (d=4, d=8).
Authors concede analytical evidence is needed for higher-dimensional resilience (Section 4.2.1).
Baselines are open-source implementations from 2016-2017; Faiss comparison is a May 2017 CPU build, and Faiss has had its own HNSW since 2018.
Loses NSW's distributed-search property: search always starts at the top layer (Discussion).
No support for element updates and removal; full 1B SIFT/DEEP not tested.
No repeats, seeds or error bars; best result per recall range chosen per algorithm.
HNSW 200M SIFT build used a special non-vectorized small-footprint build outside nmslib, so it is not the same code as other tests.
General-space tests used no custom distance functions for HNSW, causing some performance loss.
